title: How accurate is Vedic astrology? An honest answer | Ask Tota
description: The astronomy in Vedic astrology is exact to the arcsecond. Its predictions have not passed controlled tests. What the research found, and how to use it well.
og_title: How accurate is Vedic astrology, honestly
og_description: Two different questions hide inside this one. The maths is exact. The interpretations have been tested, including in India, and here is what happened.
h1: how accurate is vedic astrology? the maths is exact. the predictions are another question
dek: an astrology app saying this out loud might seem odd. but trust starts with separating the parts of jyotish u can measure from the parts u interpret, and being straight about what the research found when people tested the second part.

llms_desc: an honest look at Vedic astrology's accuracy: the astronomical calculations versus the interpretations, controlled tests (Carlson 1985, Dean and Kelly time twins 2003, Narlikar's Indian study 2009), why readings feel accurate, and how to use astrology responsibly as a reflective tool.

faq.a: the astronomical part is: planetary positions are calculated to a fraction of an arcsecond. the interpretive part, predicting personality or events from those positions, has not performed better than chance in controlled tests. many people still find it valuable for reflection.

faq.q: is vedic astrology more accurate than western astrology?
faq.a: the sidereal zodiac vedic astrology uses matches the actual constellations more closely than the tropical zodiac. that is a fact about the sky, not evidence that vedic interpretations predict better. neither system has passed controlled tests of prediction.

faq.q: has astrology ever been scientifically tested?
faq.a: yes, several times. shawn carlson's double-blind test in nature in 1985, geoffrey dean and ivan kelly's study of 2,101 time twins in 2003, and jayant narlikar's test with indian astrologers published in 2009 all found results consistent with chance.

faq.q: what was the narlikar astrology study?
faq.a: astrophysicist jayant narlikar and colleagues gave astrologers the birth charts of 200 schoolchildren, half academically gifted and half with intellectual disabilities, and asked them to tell which was which. the astrologers' results were no better than guessing.

unrelated people born within minutes of each other, so their charts are nearly identical. dean and kelly followed 2,101 people born in london in 1958 and found no more similarity between time twins across dozens of traits than chance predicts.

faq.q: why do astrology readings feel so accurate?
faq.a: several well studied effects: the forer effect, where general statements feel personal; confirmation bias, where hits are remembered and misses forgotten; and the fact that a skilled reader responds to what u tell them. none of this means readers are dishonest.

faq.q: if it is not scientifically proven, why use it?
faq.a: many people use astrology the way others use journaling or a personality framework: as a structured prompt to reflect on their life, timing and relationships. that can be valuable as long as it supports ur judgement rather than replacing it.

vedic astrology describes tendencies and timing windows, and the classical texts themselves frame results as shaped by effort. no controlled study has shown astrological predictions of specific events beat chance. treat any certain prediction as overselling.

faq.q: is the astronomy in vedic astrology correct?
faq.a: yes. modern vedic software uses ephemerides based on nasa jpl data. the sidereal calculation, with an ayanamsa such as lahiri, accounts for precession correctly.

faq.q: what should i never use astrology for?
faq.a: medical decisions, legal choices, financial bets u cannot afford to lose, mental health care, and decisions about other people's lives. those need real professionals and real information.

faq.q: why does ask tota say astrology is not proven?
faq.a: because trust depends on it. ask tota treats astrology as a traditional interpretive system people use for reflection and self-understanding. saying that clearly is better than pretending to a certainty nobody has.
jyotish has deep roots in hindu tradition as one of the six vedangas, but people of many faiths and none use it. it is better described as a traditional knowledge system than a religion.
